blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Create a scene through precise, original imagery and sensory detail; tell a narrative task from a descriptive one, and write what each needs.

blocks.heading: Imagery and the senses
blocks.text: Imagery is language that makes the reader see, hear, feel, taste or smell what is not in front of them; it works by choosing the one precise detail over the several approximate ones. Sensory detail places the reader inside a scene by reaching the senses the eye cannot: the smell of a market, the heat of a kitchen, the texture of a rope, the sound under the words. The best sensory writing does not decorate — it chooses: one true smell is worth three adjectives about atmosphere.

blocks.heading: Atmosphere
blocks.text: Atmosphere is the mood a scene’s details accumulate into — built from weather, light, sound and the behaviour of objects — and it is created by choice, not by naming the mood. The room is not "eerie"; the lamp gutters when the door opens, and the reader assembles eerie themselves. One precise image sets a mood better than a paragraph of mood-adjectives, because the image makes the reader assemble the mood — and what the reader assembles, they feel.

blocks.heading: Precise detail against adjective stacks
blocks.text: A precise detail is one exact thing noticed exactly; a pile of adjectives is several approximate things stacked in front of a noun, and the stack blurs what the one detail would have shown. "The old, cracked, grey, weathered, tired bucket" says nothing any of its five adjectives did not already half-say; "the bucket with the wire handle mended twice" makes the reader see the two mendings and, with them, the whole history of the yard. Precision is noticing; stacking is gesturing.

blocks.heading: The vague descriptive failure
blocks.text: Stacking adjectives in place of one precise detail is the descriptive failure of the vague: it multiplies the saying and never delivers the seeing, and the reader is handed effort where they wanted a picture. The cure is substitution — for every stack, find the one exact thing and keep only it — and the test is the deletion: remove an adjective, and if the noun’s picture survives, the adjective was decoration; if the picture improves, the adjective was noise.

blocks.heading: Describing and narrating
blocks.text: Descriptive writing builds a picture of a place or moment — a fixed point with a moving focus — and tells no story of events; narrative writing is a story with a character, a conflict and a change. A descriptive piece needs a fixed place or moment, a moving focus that carries the reader’s eye, precise detail, and no plot; a narrative piece needs a character, a conflict and a change. The imaginative/descriptive question has two variants — narrative and descriptive — and the variant the task’s wording signals decides what the piece must contain.

blocks.heading: The description that becomes a story
blocks.text: A description that turns into a story of events abandons its own kind: the reader arrived for a picture and is handed a plot, and the task’s named kind is part of its specification. The test is the event question — did anything happen? — and in a description the answer is no: the focus moves, the light changes, the crowd thickens, but nobody does anything that leads to anything else. A change of weather is not an event; a decision made in it is, and the description that wants one should not.

blocks.heading: Using a given sentence
blocks.text: A given opening or closing sentence is a fixed point of the brief: the piece is built out from it, if it opens, or built towards it, if it closes — and it is used word for word. The opening sentence is the exposition’s first beat: let it establish, not summarise. The closing sentence is the resolution’s last: let everything before it earn the exact words it says. The planning move for a closing sentence is to write it first — the target exists, so aim the whole piece at it.

blocks.heading: The negotiable given sentence
blocks.text: Leaving out or changing the sentence the question says the story must begin or end with breaks the brief in its most visible part: the given sentence is not a suggestion and its wording is not negotiable. The error is common because the given sentence is usually awkward — that is why it was chosen, to see what the writer builds from awkwardness. The fix is mechanical: copy the sentence at the top of the plan, build the piece to or from it, and check the draft’s first or last line against the copy, word for word.

blocks.heading: In the exam
blocks.text: The imaginative/descriptive question is one of the three Section B categories — 600–900 words, twenty-five marks, one of three questions to choose from, and the order changes from paper to paper so the question number never identifies the category. Read all three questions, choose by the kind you can write, and plan on the variant: the narrative plan is the pyramid, the descriptive plan is the moving focus. The table rewards the same five strands as the rest of Section B — and the effect the question names is part of the task, so write it at the top of the plan and keep it in view.
